boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Mine Run record (November 27 to December 2, 1863) in the Mine Run Campaign [November-December 1863], covering Payne's Farm, New Hope Church and the Mine Run lines as the frozen other names and description indicate. The November 26 crossing and the December 2 pursuit are context at the interval edges. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen structured bounds (US 69,643; CS 44,426) are imported source-reported army figures and remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen and live force fields read 114,069 total (US 69,643; CS 44,426). Humphreys gives Ewell's corps 15,650 and Hill's 17,500 enlisted men of infantry present for duty, the Second Corps 685 officers and 9,850 enlisted men of infantry per the November 30 return, and says the Second, Third and Sixth Corps together had 2,344 officers and 37,819 enlisted men of infantry against Ewell's 1,321 officers and 15,650 enlisted men. His footnote's division figures for Ewell's corps give 404, 527 and 505 officers, which sum to 1,436 (a computation here). He says Meade's best contemporary information put Lee's strength at little less than his own, while the Confederate returns show it much less. Lee says the enemy's numbers greatly exceeded Johnson's at Payne's Farm.
claims.rationale: Infantry, corps and army-level figures from returns Humphreys summarizes and did not have inspected here; they differ in scope from the frozen totals and are not adopted as matched opening strength.

claims.value: Humphreys says the country between Jacob's Ford and the turnpike was covered with dense timber and tangled undergrowth, and that the Rapidan's banks on the enemy side were over 100 feet high and very steep. At Mine Run, he says, the ravine was difficult to cross and the ground west of it was cleared for more than a thousand yards, rising gradually over a hundred feet to a summit crowned with intrenchments strengthened by abatis; he later says Warren found the works so formidable that he could not succeed. Lee calls the country almost an unbroken forest and says his army withdrew to a more favorable position west of Mine Run and strengthened it with intrenchments.
claims.rationale: Natural ground plus field works built by the defending army during the frozen interval; the works are not inherited, and no commander-created credit is assigned. No map verification.

claims.value: Humphreys says a rain-storm postponed the movement from the 24th to the 26th; the crossing was delayed two hours by the Third Corps' non-arrival and further by bridge equipage deficient one ponton at each of two fords, so the heads of columns advanced only two to four miles on the 26th. He says the army's trains had been left at Richardsville, north of the river, and that severe cold after the storm froze some pickets to death. Lee praises his troops' fortitude while lying in line of battle five days without shelter in a drenching storm and intense cold. On Rosser's raid, Lee's December 2 letter says 18 wagons, 280 mules and 150 prisoners were brought off; Humphreys, citing Rosser's report, gives eight wagons, seven ambulances, 280 mules and ninety-five prisoners.
claims.rationale: Movement and weather statements from interested accounts; no supply or transport return inspected. The raid figures conflict.

claims.value: Lee says the forest kept him from discovering whether Meade meant to advance toward Richmond or up the Rapidan on his flank, that the advance toward Orange Court-House was at first supposed to be a covering force, that Johnson did not discover the enemy until his ambulance train was fired on, and that the dense forest kept him from discovering the Union withdrawal until it was beyond pursuit. Humphreys says Early was not aware of the Jacob's Ford column until Johnson's troops were fired into, that Meade's headquarters at first could not find the forest road to French and Sedgwick and sent dispatches a distance of twelve miles or more, and that the withdrawal was made without the enemy's knowledge.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from interested accounts on both sides; the message chain was not independently inspected.

claims.value: Humphreys says Meade planned to cross the lower fords in three columns and advance rapidly, expecting to fall upon Ewell's corps before Hill's could unite with it, and later decided to attack at three points before the attack was suspended. Lee says he marched to fall on the Union flank and rear or to give battle, preferred to receive an attack rather than assume the offensive, and prepared to attack on the morning of December 2. NPS says Meade attempted to steal a march through the Wilderness and strike the Confederate right flank.
claims.rationale: Stated plans and intent; not a causal estimate.

claims.value: Humphreys says the plan required prompt, vigorous action and intelligent compliance from subordinate commanders; that French halted at Morris's, remained on the defensive with three times Johnson's force, and in effect paralyzed the whole army; that Warren suspended his November 30 attack, whereupon Sedgwick's was suspended; that the plan of attack was the only one usable but necessarily vicious; and that Meade acknowledged the movement a failure. Lee credits Johnson's promptness in meeting the unexpected attack. The frozen commanders are General Robert E. Lee and Major General George G. Meade; the live page heads Lee as Major General, which is not adopted.
claims.rationale: Attributed judgments from interested accounts; the frozen commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Inconclusive; the live result reads Indecisive. At Payne's Farm, Lee says Johnson drove the enemy back through the woods but could not follow up; Humphreys says the Third Corps line advanced again, forced the enemy back and repulsed a second attack; NPS says Johnson's counterattack was scattered by heavy fire and broken terrain. Lee says his planned December 2 attack was prevented by the Union retreat; NPS says Meade retired during the night of December 1–2, ending the winter campaign.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The Payne's Farm accounts conflict.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 1,952 total (US 1,272; CS 680); the live field reads 2428 total (US 1633; CS 795). Humphreys gives the Third Corps' loss at Payne's Farm, from French's report, as 952 and Johnson's division's as 498, and calls other casualties small. Lee gives Johnson's total loss as 545 and his other casualties as slight. Lee says about 500 prisoners were taken; Humphreys says the pursuers picked up some 200 and some 300 stragglers.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Johnson's loss differs between Humphreys and Lee.

open_questions: French's, Early's, Johnson's, Warren's and Sedgwick's reports, the Confederate field return (No. 99, garbled in OCR) and the Union returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Humphreys is an interested history by the Army of the Potomac's chief of staff in 1863–64, per his publisher's list. Lee's telegrams, letters and report, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXIX, Part 1, are a separate family of an interested Confederate commander's accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
